description: We are a student team interested in space and technology. We enjoy exploring ideas, and creating something together. By joining NASA Space Apps Challenge, we want to improve ourselves, share our ideas, and develop a meaningful project as a team. We are open to researching, learning from each other, and finding creative solutions to different problems. For us, this competition is not just about competing, but also about gaining experience, meeting new people, and having fun along the way.
summary: Our team developed 'Parlayan Yıldızlar: Mars Map,' an advanced multi-layered Geographic Information System (GIS) and integrated wrist-mounted hardware designed to ensure safe astronaut navigation on Mars. To address the challenge of unpredictable Martian hazards, our software utilizes real NASA orbital datasets (MOLA, HRSC, Viking) to render real-time telemetry overlays. Astronauts can dynamically toggle between Topographic, Optical, Thermal, and Radiation map layers based on current environmental conditions. A key feature is our Autonomous Safe Pathfinding Algorithm, which continuously integrates suit telemetry with surface slope and radiation data to compute the safest traverse corridors, actively avoiding steep craters and high-radiation zones. Paired with extreme-environment hardware powered by a redundant betavoltaic battery system, this mapping solution is critical for survival. It allows astronauts to navigate safely even during zero-visibility dust storms, maximizing mission safety and operational autonomy.
details:
Interplanetary Survival Guide is a proposed astronaut safety and navigation system designed to support crewed missions on the surface of Mars. Developed by Team Parlayan Yıldızlar, the project combines an ergonomic wrist-mounted navigation device called SENTRA (Space Environmental Navigation & Threat Response Assistant) with a multi-layered Geographic Information System (GIS) called Parlayan Yıldızlar: Mars Map.

The system is designed to help astronauts explore the Martian surface while monitoring environmental conditions and avoiding potential hazards. It focuses on the Elysium Planitia region and the InSight landing site. By integrating NASA MOLA, HRSC, Viking MDIM21, and InSight datasets, the mapping interface provides topographic, optical, thermal, and radiation information. It also includes wind visualization to help astronauts understand changing environmental conditions. Users can select locations on the map to examine important information such as temperature, atmospheric pressure, radiation levels, and surface elevation before deciding where to travel.

One of the project's key features is its temperature-based warning system. It compares surface temperatures with predefined safety limits and alerts astronauts when an area may be dangerous. In addition, the proposed autonomous pathfinding algorithm considers terrain slopes, radiation levels, and astronaut suit telemetry, including remaining oxygen and power reserves, to identify safer routes rather than simply choosing the shortest path.

The wrist-mounted device is designed with materials suitable for the harsh Martian environment. Its proposed construction includes cryogenic PEEK for the outer casing, Aluminum 7075-T6 for the internal structure, synthetic sapphire glass for screen protection, and Indium Tin Oxide (ITO) for the touchscreen layer. Its hybrid power architecture combines a solid-state primary battery with a betavoltaic emergency backup cell, intended to maintain essential functions such as location tracking and emergency beacon operation if the main power source fails.

Our project is creative because it integrates wearable technology, planetary mapping, environmental monitoring, hazard detection, and autonomous route planning into a single astronaut-support system. It also considers challenging situations such as extreme nighttime cold and dust storms, providing alternative navigation features to help astronauts reach a safe habitat.

The main intended impact is to improve astronaut safety, increase environmental awareness, reduce exposure to dangerous areas, and support more independent and reliable exploration of the Martian surface.
